claims.text: Active-learning-driven sampling will substantially reduce the number of high-cost molecular-dynamics evaluations required for ab initio free-energy calculations.
The proposed method will accurately retain vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling in both solid and liquid phases near melting.
The proposed method will not significantly sacrifice fidelity relative to full ab initio molecular dynamics.
The intended scope includes elemental materials, binary alloys, and multicomponent high-entropy alloys in solid and liquid states near their melting points.
The intervention adaptively selects the most informative atomic configurations along free-energy integration paths for full ab initio evaluation.
A trained surrogate model will estimate unsampled regions of the integration paths.
The targeted integration paths account for vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling under high-temperature conditions near fusion.
The solid–liquid free-energy integration path controls accurate determination of entropy contributions and phase free energies.
Active learning can identify configurations where local energetic and vibrational environments change most strongly.
Selecting those configurations will minimize redundant DFT evaluations while maintaining accurate free-energy differences.
The method could provide a 2–5× computational speedup.
Phase free energies will remain within approximately 10 meV/atom of explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics and TOR-TILD results.
The resulting free energies will accurately reproduce observables such as melting temperature.
TOR-TILD is effective for elemental and binary systems but becomes prohibitively expensive for complex high-entropy alloys.
The method is expected to work for systems containing five or more principal elements near their fusion temperatures.
Performance outside high-temperature regimes and in extremely compositionally complex systems is untested.
The speedup and retained accuracy may vary with material complexity and with the efficiency of configuration selection.
The hypothesis is falsified if free-energy differences deviate by more than approximately 10 meV/atom from full ab initio molecular dynamics or if the speedup is less than 2×.
